candidates.name: GPO Museum
candidates.content: The GPO is the headquarters of the Post Office in Ireland, built in Neo-Classical style 1814-1818. In 1916 it was occupied by Irish rebels led by PH Pearse, who read the Proclamation of the Republic outside the front door of the b

candidates.name: Hugh Lane Gallery
candidates.content: Sir Hugh Lane (1875-1915) was one of the first collectors of modern art. He died in the sinking of Lusitania and this public gallery reflects his Will, which involved about as much negotiation, fudge and compromise as the Treaty f

candidates.name: EPIC The Irish Emigration Museum
candidates.price: Adult €21, child 6-12 €10.50, teen 13-17 €14.50, under 5s free, senior €19
candidates.content: Over the centuries more than 10 million people emigrated from Ireland; this is the story of why they left, where they went and how they shaped the world.

candidates.name: National Gallery of Ireland
candidates.hours: Tue Wed Fri Sat 9:15AM-5:30PM, Thu 9:15AM-8:30PM, Sun Mon 11AM-5:30PM
candidates.content: Impressive national collection of Irish and European Art. In January the gallery displays its watercolours by JMW Turner; the original donor specified that they had to be kept out of the light for the rest of the year.

candidates.name: National Museum of Ireland - Archaeology
candidates.content: Amazing display of Ireland's artefacts from prehistory through the Viking era to independence. The standout is the Treasury (with the 12th century Ardagh Chalice and 9th century Tara Brooch), and the prehistoric jewellery: gold an

candidates.name: Dublin Castle
candidates.content: Former seat of British rule in Ireland. The guided tour takes in the medieval basements and Chapel Royal, then you see the State Apartments in your own time. You can skip the tour and just see the apartments for less.

candidates.name: Chester Beatty Library
candidates.hours: Mar-Oct Mon Tue Thu-Sat 10AM-5:30PM, Wed 10AM-8PM, Sun noon-5:30PM, Nov-Feb closed Mon
candidates.content: Sir Alfred Chester Beatty (1875-1968) was an American mining magnate who amassed a fabulous collection of early books and manuscripts and oriental art. He moved to London and collaborated generously with the British Museum, but in

candidates.name: Christ Church Cathedral
candidates.hours: Apr-Sep Mon-Sat 9:30AM-7PM, Sun 12:30-14:30PM & 4:30-7PM; Oct-Mar Mon-Sat 9:30AM-5PM, Sun 12:30-2:30PM
candidates.content: A wooden church was built by the Vikings around 1030, and the first stone church was from the 1180s. So this is the oldest building in Dublin, though it underwent a massive restoration in the 1870s. It became Protestant under Hent

candidates.name: National Museum of Ireland - Decorative Arts & History
candidates.content: The building is remarkable, a Georgian barracks around a parade square. Displays decorative arts and artefacts over 400 years, from rustic houses through Georgian elegance to "Proclaiming a Republic", the events of Easter 1916 whe

candidates.name: Kilmainham Gaol
candidates.content: This prison was in use 1796-1924; thousands have passed through, including many convicts transported to Australia. It's best known as the place where the rebels from the 1916 Easter Rising were executed. (Several now lie in Arbour

candidates.name: Glasnevin Cemetery
candidates.content: This opened as an RC cemetery in 1832, in an era when the Catholics weren't allowed their own parish churches, and their burials were begrudged affairs in Protestant ground. Glasnevin has grown and grown, expanding south across Fi

candidates.name: St Mary's Pro-Cathedral
candidates.content: Dublin's Catholic cathedral, built in 1825. Catholicism was always the majority religion in Ireland, but its practice was forbidden until the 19th century. The official cathedral is Christ Church, so designated by the Pope in 1300

candidates.name: National Museum of Ireland - Natural History
candidates.hours: closed for refurbishment as of April 2026, but some of the collections are on display in the Dead Zoo Lab at their Collins Barracks site
candidates.content: The "Dead Zoo" contains a comprehensive zoological collection presented in a manner unchanged since its establishment in Victorian times.

candidates.name: Irish Museum of Modern Art
candidates.content: Modern and contemporary art, housed in the Royal Hospital of 1684. See also the elegant courtyard and formal gardens.

candidates.name: National Botanic Gardens
candidates.hours: Mar-Oct Mon-Fri 9AM-5PM, Sat Sun 10AM-6PM; Nov-Feb Mon-Fri 9AM-4:30PM, Sat Sun 10AM-4:30PM
candidates.content: Extensive gardens favouring alkaline-loving species. The great Palm House was where Wittgenstein often came to warm his lugubrious backside. A gateway leads into Glasnevin Cemetery adjacent. The gardens also manage the arboretum a

candidates.name: National Leprechaun Museum
candidates.content: The "little folk" appeared in lore around 1300 AD but only flourished from the 19th century Celtic revival, dressed in late Georgian garb in an idealised rural past, mending a shoe. They proliferated into the silliest of 20th cent

candidates.name: Irish Whiskey Museum
candidates.content: And not before time. Irish distilleries have for too long pumped out bland commercial fare, though the country has all the ingredients and know-how to produce whiskey of character to rival single-malt Scotch.

candidates.name: Little Museum of Dublin
candidates.content: Their main building on St Stephen's Green is closed for renovation, so this is a temporary home. It displays the 20th-century social, cultural and political history of Dublin city, with many artefacts donated by Dubliners. Visit b

candidates.name: Irish Jewish Museum
candidates.content: Exhibiting Jewish life in the cities - as in Great Britain, many were emigres from "White Russia". Their best known member is fictional, Leopold Bloom the protagonist of Ulysses.

candidates.name: St Patrick's Cathedral
candidates.content: Founded in 1191, it became Anglican at the Reformation, so the Protestants had two cathedrals in the same city while the Catholics had none. It feuded with Christ Church over rights and precedence, until 1871 when Christ Church wa

candidates.name: Dublin Zoo
candidates.content: Opened in 1830 and extended in 1997, this Zoo has a dozen habitats and is the largest in Ireland.

candidates.name: Pearse Museum
candidates.content: Patrick Pearse (1879-1916) saw Irish culture and language as essential for national independence. His one and only case as a barrister was his unsuccessful defence of a Donegal tradesman for using an "illegible" sign, and the verd

candidates.name: Green on Red Gallery
candidates.content: Commercial gallery exhibiting Irish and international modern art.

candidates.name: Leinster House
candidates.content: This opulent Georgian mansion is in the same block as the Archaeology Museum. Designed by Cassels, it was built in 1745 as the residence of the Duke of Leinster at a time when the southside was unfashionable. It proved an "anchor

candidates.name: Rathfarnham Castle
candidates.content: Built as a fortified mansion around 1583 and prettified in the 18th century, it fell derelict in the 19th but has been restored as a museum.

candidates.name: The Jeanie Johnston
candidates.content: One million Irish people fled Ireland during the famine. 2500 took a gruelling voyage aboard the Jeanie Johnston, and this is a replica. You take a 50 min tour above and below deck.

candidates.name: 14 Henrietta Street
candidates.content: Many Dubliners lived in buildings like this. Built in the 1740s, its first occupant was Lord Viscount Molesworth and his family, and after him came a series of Right Honorable This and Viscount That and Bishop of Wherever. But the

candidates.name: Trinity College
candidates.hours: Kells: May-Sep Mon-Sat 8:30AM-7PM, Sun 9:30AM-5PM; Oct-Apr Mon-Sat 9:30AM-5PM, Sun noon-4:30PM
candidates.content: Trinity College is the fine Georgian campus of the University of Dublin. It's generally open to stroll around in daylight hours, but it is a working university, and most interiors are off-limits to tourists. You can visit the Chap

candidates.name: Guinness Storehouse
candidates.content: Guinness is brewed in 49 countries and Ireland just happens to be one of them. The St James Gate brewery is still in production, now part of Diageo, and this vast storehouse has become an exhibition (self-guided) on the drink and

candidates.name: Teeling Distillery
candidates.price: Tasting tour €25 (pointless going for the cheaper "cocktail" tour)
candidates.content: Distillery opened in 2015, primarily for whiskey but with small amounts of poitín.

candidates.name: Gate Theatre
candidates.content: This has a focus on European and American theatre ranging from classics to modern plays. It was established as a theatre company in 1928 by Hilton Edward and Micheál MacLiammóir.

candidates.name: Bord Gáis Energy Theatre
candidates.content: The theatre offers a wide range of shows featuring ballet, musicals, family shows, drama, concerts, comedy and opera. With a 2100-seater auditorium, the building was designed by Daniel Libeskind and completed in 2010.

candidates.name: Croke Park Stadium
candidates.content: This stages Gaelic football and hurling for Dublin County GAA and national competitions, with a playing season April-Sep. The stadium has a capacity of 82,300 yet you may struggle to get tickets for big games. Tours of the stadium

candidates.name: Leopardstown Racecourse
candidates.content: This has regular meetings throughout the year, flat-racing in summer and jumps in winter. There's a "Pay as you Play" golf course within the racecourse grounds, as well as bars, restaurants and a nightclub.

candidates.name: Gaiety Theatre
candidates.content: Founded in 1871 so this is the oldest continually operating theatre in Dublin. It hosts popular musical shows, opera, ballet, dance and drama.

candidates.name: Jameson Distillery
candidates.content: Jameson whiskey was produced in Dublin from 1780 to 1976, when the business relocated to Midleton near Cork. So the old Bow St distillery no longer makes whiskey but has been converted into a museum about the process and industry.

candidates.name: Dublin Literary Pub Crawl
candidates.content: This is the most ingenious crash course in Irish literature, history, architecture and pub bonhomie yet devised... It combines street theatre with the 'craic' that makes Dublin pubs the liveliest in Europe. It is a highly enjoyabl

candidates.name: Abbey Theatre
candidates.content: Opened in 1904, and always at the centre of the Irish drama scene, the Abbey is a good venue for catching local playwrights' work but with a global repertoire. It's intended to replace the current building with two new theatres fr

candidates.name: The Lazy Bike Tour Company
candidates.content: Two-hour bike tours of the major sights and off the beaten track, with informative guides.

candidates.name: Walking Tours
candidates.content: Dublin city is famous for its characters. A great way to experience and live the city is by learning about it from people who are characters themselves - Dublin Tour Guides. Tours can vary from one to four hours in length and incl

candidates.name: National Concert Hall
candidates.content: This offers classical concerts. Frequent performances by the resident orchestra, the RTÉ National Symphony Orchestra. The main auditorium seats 1200 and there are three smaller spaces. It was built in 1865 for a trade fair then be

candidates.name: The Helix
candidates.content: Event venue and theatre located in the northern suburbs of the city, built in 1996. Hosts a wide variety of talks and performances.

candidates.name: Leinster Rugby
candidates.content: Leinster play in the United Rugby Championship, the professional European league, and often win it. The stadium has a capacity of 18,500 and big games sometimes transfer to Aviva stadium.

candidates.name: Shamrock Rovers
candidates.content: They play in the League of Ireland Premier Division, the top tier. The stadium (capacity 10,500) is on N81 two km west of M50.

candidates.name: Conradh na Gaeilge
candidates.content: Cultural centre where Irish is the first language. They organise events and classes.

candidates.name: Irish Film Institute
candidates.content: Arthouse cinema for independent Irish and international movies.

candidates.name: Peadar Kearney's
candidates.content: Named for Peadar Ó Cearnaígh (1883-1942) who penned Amhráin na bhFiann, Ireland's national anthem, and was uncle to the three Behans, authors and prolific drinkers all. The pub is a great spot for pre- and post-gig drinks next to

candidates.name: Frank Ryans
candidates.content: This pub and pizzeria has friendly bar staff and a mixed crowd of students, law types, trendies and locals. Expect weekly trad nights interspersed with Rockabilly, Country and Soul on the jukebox.

candidates.name: The Brazen Head
candidates.content: Surely the oldest pub in Dublin, founded in 1198 - Ireland's oldest, in Athlone, is from 900 AD. Wonderful on warm, dry summer nights. Live trad music and friendly atmosphere. One of the bars is covered in signed currency notes, t

candidates.name: Against the Grain
candidates.content: Owned by a Galway brewery, this has a wide variety of Irish micro-brews and world beers. No generic commercial beers on tap. A vibrant pub with an eclectic clientele.

candidates.name: JR Mahon's
candidates.content: Spread over two stories, they produce a very good stout quite different to Guinness, fresher and more complex, plus their own ale and lager. Also has good cafeteria-style lunch.

candidates.name: Porterhouse
candidates.content: Indigenous brews including an oyster stout, plus an extensive Belgian and international beer list. Also does reasonably priced food. Has sister pubs on Grafton St and in Bray and Phibsboro.

candidates.name: Bruxelles
candidates.content: Lively pub founded in 1886. Spread over 3 bars the music is loud and the atmosphere is buzzing. Outside is a statue of Phil Lynott, from Irish rock band Thin Lizzy. For metal, rock and indie music go downstairs.

candidates.name: The Workmans Club
candidates.content: From 1888 to 2003 this was the city's Working Mens Club, turning into a live entertainment venue in 2010. It's on two floors, the main live room is 300 capacity and beside it is the venue bar. It's friendly, relaxing and well-run.

candidates.name: The Cobblestone
candidates.content: They describe themselves as "a drinking pub with a music problem" and have nightly trad sessions.

candidates.name: O'Donoghue's
candidates.content: With two bars across a courtyard, it's famous for impromptu live music, and where folk group The Dubliners were formed. They have rooms.

candidates.name: The Barge
candidates.content: Friendly trad pub with four areas, good food and great decor.

candidates.name: Hartigan's
candidates.content: Popular student bar, good choice after international rugby matches.

candidates.name: Ned O'Shea's
candidates.content: Decent food and live music and dancing. Ned O’Shea (1937-2018) was a famous trad musician from Kerry.

candidates.name: John Fallon's
candidates.content: Small friendly local pub.

candidates.name: Bewley's Café
candidates.content: Grand stylish coffee shop, a Dublin institution. It's had some famous regular customers, from Joyce to Geldof, but they'll make you feel just as important.

candidates.name: Butlers Chocolate Café
candidates.content: Chain of chocolate-themed cafes, Wicklow Street is the original outlet. There are three others in city centre, plus airside in T1 and T2 at the airport. They also ship orders.

candidates.name: Gallagher's Boxty House
candidates.content: Good traditional Irish fare and not expensive. A boxty is a traditional Irish potato pancake filled and rolled up. Also try the Irish stew and the chowder. Small, friendly, traditional Irish decor.

candidates.name: Lemon Crèpe & Coffee Company
candidates.content: Good value filled crèpes, they also do waffles and sandwiches.

candidates.name: Govinda's
candidates.content: Hare Krishna-run vegetarian restaurant. Filling portions, only order their Special if you're really hungry.

candidates.name: Pablo Picante
candidates.content: Small friendly Mexican eatery, eat in or take away to nearby St Stephen's Green. They also have outlets at Clarendon Market and Dawson St.

candidates.name: Zaytoon
candidates.content: Casual Persian restaurant. They also have a fast-food cafe in Temple Bar (corner of Parliament St and Essex St).

candidates.name: Salamanca
candidates.content: Good value, tasty and substantial tapas, sized more like raciones.

candidates.name: Bang Restaurant
candidates.hours: Mon–Tue 5–9:30PM, Wed-Fri noon–3PM and 5–9:30PM, Sat 1–4PM and 4–10:30PM
candidates.content: A great cosmopolitan menu. Not cheap, but food and presentation is excellent.

candidates.name: Caketopia
candidates.price: Cakes starting at 70€ serving up to 10 people
candidates.content: Artisan home-made cakes for any occasion for collection or delivery all over Dublin and surrounding areas.

candidates.name: Elephant & Castle
candidates.content: Famous and popular for its chicken wings, you could have a long wait for a table Saturday lunchtime. It's now a national chain but this is the original outlet.

candidates.name: Bad Ass Café
candidates.content: Modern pub and entertainment venue for US-themed food, plus trad Irish beer and live music.

december.text: Special rate (Sa Su midnight-4AM, 24 Dec 8PM through Christmas to 8AM 26 Dec, 31 Dec 8PM to 8AM 1 Jan): same as Premium rate but after flagfall you go straight to Tariff B, there's no Tariff A.
